title: C. elegans Differential Expression Analysis
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter works through an end-to-end differential gene expression analysis of an embryonic *C. elegans* RNA-seq experiment using the Bioconductor package `edgeR`. It takes as input gene-level read counts obtained from read alignment, covers sample metadata handling, library size normalization via TMM, exploratory data analysis via multidimensional scaling, low-count filtering, negative binomial dispersion estimation, and diagnostic visualization. ## Biological Context and Experimental Design In *Caenorhabditis elegans*, the very first mitotic division of the single-cell zygote is asymmetric: it cleaves into a larger anterior blastomere, termed **AB**, and a smaller posterior blastomere, termed **P1**. These two daughter cells possess radically different developmental fates, producing distinct somatic and germline lineages. Because this division takes place prior to the major onset of zygotic transcription, differences in transcript abundance between the two blastomeres reflect differential inheritance, selective maternal mRNA degradation, or localized stability. To characterize these transcript distributions, researchers hand-dissected and pooled isolated AB and P1 blastomeres across replicates and profiled them using standard bulk RNA-seq. Reads from this study were previously aligned against the *C. elegans* reference genome and summarized into gene-level counts using the `Rsubread` package. The resulting count matrix and associated sample metadata form the starting point for statistical modeling. ## Constructing the Count Object and Metadata Analysis begins in R using the `edgeR` package (which internally depends on `limma`). ```r library(edgeR) ``` The count matrix produced by `Rsubread::featureCounts` is extracted into a `DGEList` (Digital Gene Expression List) object, the core data structure used throughout `edgeR`: ```r dge <- DGEList(fc$counts) ``` Before proceeding, verify that the column order of the count matrix strictly matches the row order of the sample metadata sheet (`target`): ```r substr(colnames(dge), 1, 10) == target$Run ## [1] TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE ``` With sample integrity confirmed across all six sequencing runs, assign informative column names combining the cell type and replicate index, and define the biological condition as an experimental factor: ```r colnames(dge) <- paste0(target$`cell type:ch1`, target$`replicate:ch1`) cellType <- as.factor(target$`cell type:ch1`) ``` Here, `cellType` partitions the six samples into two groups: the anterior blastomere (AB) and the posterior blastomere (P1), each represented by biological replicates. ## Composition Normalization Sequencing depth varies from library to library due to technical factors in library preparation and sequencing. Furthermore, RNA-seq data measures relative, not absolute, abundance. If a small subset of genes is expressed at extremely high levels in one condition, those transcripts consume sequencing real estate, making all other genes appear artificially downregulated—a phenomenon termed composition bias. To correct for both library size differences and compositional distortions, `edgeR` uses the **Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM)** method: ```r dge <- calcNormFactors(dge) ``` The TMM algorithm designates one sample as a reference and calculates scaling factors $f_k$ for every library $k$. It does this by taking the weighted mean of log-fold changes (the $M$-values) across genes, trimming away the genes with the highest and lowest log ratios, as well as those with extreme absolute expression levels ($A$-values). The effective library size for sample $k$ then becomes: $$N_k^* = N_k \cdot f_k$$ where $N_k$ is the raw library size (total sequenced reads mapped for that sample). ## Exploratory Data Analysis: Multidimensional Scaling High-dimensional gene expression profiles can be summarized and visualized using **multidimensional scaling (MDS)**. The objective of MDS is to construct a low-dimensional (typically two-dimensional) projection of the samples such that pairwise geometric distances in the plane match pairwise sample distances as closely as possible. In `edgeR`, the function `plotMDS` calculates pairwise distances defined as the root-mean-square of the leading $\log_2$-fold changes between each pair of samples. By default, this distance is computed over the top 500 genes exhibiting the largest variation between that specific sample pair: ```r plotMDS(dge, top = 500, col = as.double(cellType)) ``` The leading dimension (Dimension 1) clearly separates the AB blastomeres from the P1 blastomeres, demonstrating that the primary driver of transcriptional variance is the biological divergence between the anterior and posterior cells. Replicate variability is captured along Dimension 2. ## Filtering Low-Count Genes Genes with near-zero counts across all libraries provide negligible statistical power for detecting differential expression while inflating the multiple testing burden. Moreover, estimating dispersion parameters on zero-inflated counts can be unstable. We construct a design matrix reflecting the experimental contrast between cell types and filter features using `filterByExpr`: ```r design <- model.matrix(~cellType) keep <- filterByExpr(dge, design) dge <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] ``` The function `filterByExpr` retains genes that achieve a minimum threshold of Counts Per Million (CPM) in a sufficient number of samples (determined automatically by the smallest group sample size in the design matrix). Setting `keep.lib.sizes = FALSE` instructs `edgeR` to recalculate library sizes as the column sums of the retained count matrix rather than retaining the original, unfiltered sequencing depths. Because removing low-count genes alters total counts per sample, composition normalization factors must be recalculated: ```r dge <- calcNormFactors(dge) ``` ## Modeling and Dispersion Estimation ### The Negative Binomial Model For RNA-seq data, the variance of read counts $Y_{gi}$ for gene $g$ in sample $i$ exceeds the mean $\mu_{gi}$—a property termed **overdispersion**. While a standard Poisson model forces $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \operatorname{E}(Y)$, `edgeR` models counts using a Negative Binomial (NB) distribution: $$Y_{gi} \sim \text{NB}(\mu_{gi}, \phi_g)$$ with mean and variance parameterizations: $$\operatorname{E}(Y_{gi}) = \mu_{gi} = N_i^* \exp(x_i^T \beta_g)$$ $$\operatorname{Var}(Y_{gi}) = \mu_{gi} + \phi_g \mu_{gi}^2$$ Here, $\phi_g \ge 0$ represents the **dispersion** of gene $g$. The square root of the dispersion parameter corresponds to the **Biological Coefficient of Variation (BCV)**: $$\text{BCV}_g = \sqrt{\phi_g} = \frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y_{gi}) - \mu_{gi}}}{\mu_{gi}}$$ BCV represents the coefficient of variation with which the true biological abundance of a gene fluctuates between biological replicates, isolating biological variance from technical Poisson shot noise. ### Estimating Dispersions Because RNA-seq experiments typically feature small sample sizes (such as $n = 3$ per group), gene-specific estimates of $\phi_g$ suffer from severe estimation uncertainty. `edgeR` uses an empirical Bayes approach that shrinks gene-wise dispersions toward a global mean-dispersion trend: ```r dge <- estimateDisp(dge, design) plotBCV(dge) ``` The function `estimateDisp` computes: 1. A **common dispersion** pooled across all genes. 2. A **trended dispersion** that captures the systematic relationship between average abundance and dispersion. 3. A **tagwise dispersion** that shrinks individual gene estimates toward the trend line by borrowing information across all features. The resulting diagnostic plot illustrates typical RNA-seq behavior: genes with low average counts exhibit higher, more variable BCVs due to technical noise and lower counting precision, whereas highly expressed genes plateau near a stable biological baseline. Empirical Bayes shrinkage dampens extreme, unreliable gene-level dispersion estimates back toward the fitted trend line, stabilizing downstream differential expression testing. ## Sources - *NOTES: Elegans: DE analysis* (Lieven Clement, 27 October 2019): sections on reading featurecounts, sample metadata association, normalization, MDS visualization, low-count filtering, and dispersion estimation (`estimateDisp`, `plotBCV`). - Reference to read alignment and gene-level summarization performed in the preceding `Rsubread` tutorial (not contained in supplied text).
